title: Learning to Discover at Test Time
claim: Continued test-time training shifts the reward distribution toward better solutions, surpassing the prior best, while fixed-policy best-of-N sampling stays stuck at poor ones.
layout: 1 panel, left-to-right slow-to-fast axis, overlaid density curves with dashed reference lines
description: A single wide horizontal plot of overlaid density curves along a runtime axis. The axis is labeled GPUMode TriMul Competition Kernel Runtime (H100), running from Slowest on the left to Fastest on the right. At the far left, a gray and black best-of-N distribution (policy pi_theta_0) forms two tall peaks. Blue TTT-Discover distributions at steps 9, 24 and 49 appear as progressively lower, wider humps moving rightward. Each is annotated with the policy symbol and a short italic note: mixed precision, fusing all core operations, deeper fusion. Vertical dashed lines mark Best-of-25600 (5352µs), 5th Human (3655µs) and Best Human (1371µs). A dashed blue line marks the best TTT-Discover result (1161µs), beyond the human best. A legend sits at top center. The eye goes first to the tall left peaks, then follows the blue humps rightward.
caption: TTT-Discover continues to train an LLM on a single problem at test time. πθi denotes the policy with the updates weights at test-time training step i. We plot the reward distribution at step 0, 9, 24, and 49 (final), recorded while test-time training for the GPUMode TriMul competition. We generate 512 solutions at each step. As training progresses, the LLM generates better solutions that ultimately surpass the prior art (best human). For comparison, we plot the reward distribution of best-of-N with the same total sampling budget.
abstract: How can we use AI to discover a new state of the art for a scientific problem? Prior work in test-time scaling, such as AlphaEvolve, performs search by prompting a frozen LLM. We perform reinforcement learning at test time, so the LLM can continue to train, but now with experience specific to the test problem. This form of continual learning is quite special, because its goal is to produce one great solution rather than many good ones on average, and to solve this very problem rather than generalize to other problems. Therefore, our learning objective and search subroutine are designed to prioritize the most promising solutions. We call this method Test-Time Training to Discover (TTT-Discover). Following prior work, we focus on problems with continuous rewards. We report results for every problem we attempted, across mathematics, GPU kernel engineering, algorithm design, and biology. TTT-Discover sets the new state of the art in almost all of them: (i) ErdÅs' minimum overlap problem and an autocorrelation inequality; (ii) a GPUMode kernel competition (up to $2\times$ faster than prior art); (iii) past AtCoder algorithm competitions; and (iv) denoising problem in single-cell analysis. Our solutions are reviewed by experts or the organizers. All our results are achieved with an open model, OpenAI gpt-oss-120b, and can be reproduced with our publicly available code, in contrast to previous best results that required closed frontier models. Our test-time training runs are performed using Tinker, an API by Thinking Machines, with a cost of only a few hundred dollars per problem.
